title: Qualified Intermediary Coordination
name: Qualified Intermediary Coordination
metaTitle: Qualified Intermediary Coordination in Denver, CO
metaDescription: Coordinating with your qualified intermediary and Denver-area title companies so exchange funds, documents, and closing dates line up on schedule.

sections.html: The qualified intermediary holds the exchange funds and prepares the exchange agreement, but somebody still has to keep the QI, the title company, the buyer's lender, and the closing schedule all moving on the same calendar. That's the piece we handle. We don't act as your QI and we don't give tax advice; we make sure the paperwork and the property search stay in sync so the QI has what it needs when it needs it.

sections.heading: What we coordinate day to day
sections.html: Once a relinquished property is under contract, we confirm the QI is engaged before closing, since the exchange agreement has to be signed prior to the sale closing for the exchange to work. From there we track replacement property paperwork, purchase agreements, title commitments, and lender documents, and route copies to the QI as each piece comes together. If a Denver title company needs a signed identification letter before releasing exchange funds for a purchase, we make sure that letter is in hand before the closing date, not the morning of.

sections.heading: Working with Denver-area title and escrow
sections.html: Most title companies operating in metro Denver handle 1031 closings routinely, but timelines still get tight when a RiNo or LoDo apartment deal closes on an accelerated schedule set by a motivated seller. We stay in contact with the closing team on both sides of the exchange so fund transfers from the QI's escrow account match the actual closing date instead of getting scheduled a day or two off, which can create a mechanical delay that has nothing to do with the exchange itself but still costs an investor time.

sections.heading: Common coordination gaps we catch
sections.html:
A few issues come up often enough that we check for them on every file:

  • Exchange agreement signed after the relinquished property closing instead of before
  • Identification notice sent to the wrong party or missing a signature
  • Replacement property purchase contract naming the investor instead of the QI as buyer
  • Wire instructions mismatched between the QI's bank and the title company
  • Closing date set without confirming exchange funds will be available that day

sections.heading: Where the 180-day period gets squeezed
sections.html: The 180-day exchange period runs from the relinquished property closing, not from when a replacement property is identified, so time spent negotiating a purchase contract in a competitive Denver submarket eats directly into that window. We keep a running countdown for every active file so an investor and their QI both know exactly how many days remain before a final decision has to close.

sections.heading: Confirming with your own advisors
sections.html: We're not the qualified intermediary and we don't file Form 8824 or give tax advice. Everything we coordinate gets confirmed against the investor's actual QI agreement and their tax advisor's guidance before a closing date is locked in, since the QI and the investor's CPA are the two parties with authority over exchange mechanics and reporting.

sections.heading: What we ask an investor to have ready
sections.html:
Before a relinquished property even goes on the market, we ask investors to have their QI selected and the exchange agreement reviewed, since some sellers and title companies want confirmation that a QI is in place before they'll finalize a purchase contract that mentions an exchange. Waiting until a week before closing to pick a QI has caused avoidable delays on more than one Denver file, especially when a lender also needs its own paperwork reviewed against the exchange structure at the same time.

We also ask investors early whether they've used a QI before, since a first-time exchange investor usually needs a bit more explanation of how the escrow account works and why they never touch the sale proceeds directly, while a repeat investor's file tends to move faster because the mechanics are already familiar.

We also keep a written record of every deadline and hand-off on a file instead of relying on a mental list, so if a different person on our team or the QI's team picks up the coordination mid-exchange, nothing falls through because the original contact was out for a week.

faqs.q: Do you act as our qualified intermediary?
faqs.a: No. We coordinate the moving pieces around your QI, title company, and closing schedule, but the QI itself has to be a separate, independent party under the exchange rules. We work alongside whichever QI you've engaged.

faqs.q: What happens if the exchange agreement gets signed after the relinquished property closes?
faqs.a: That timing generally disqualifies the exchange, since the agreement has to be in place before the sale closes. We check this on every file specifically because it's one of the most common and costly mistakes we see.

faqs.q: How do you keep a Denver title company and the QI's escrow account in sync?
faqs.a: We confirm wire instructions and closing dates with both parties ahead of the closing rather than the day of, and we flag any mismatch in timing before funds are scheduled to move.

faqs.q: Does the 180-day exchange period start when I identify a replacement property?
faqs.a: No, it starts on the closing date of your relinquished property. Identification happens within the first 45 days of that same 180-day window, not on a separate clock.

faqs.q: Can you help if my exchange agreement or identification notice has an error in it?
faqs.a: We can flag issues we notice, like a missing signature or a notice sent to the wrong party, but corrections to exchange documents need to go through your qualified intermediary and, where relevant, your tax advisor.
